title: Evaluating sources
note: Professional fact-checkers read laterally: before trusting a page, they leave it and see what others say about the source. Mike Caulfield's SIFT packs this into four moves: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.

read.title: Reading sideways
text: When people judge an unfamiliar website, most do what they were taught: they study the page itself. They read the About section, look at the design, and check whether it cites sources. Sam Wineburg's research group at Stanford found that this kind of vertical reading often fails, because a polished site with an official-sounding name can be run by a lobbying group or a single motivated person.

Professional fact-checkers did something different. Within seconds they opened new tabs and searched for the organization, its funders, and what reliable outlets said about it. This is lateral reading: you learn about a source by leaving it.

Mike Caulfield built the habit into four moves called SIFT. Stop and notice whether you know the source. Investigate the source, briefly, before reading closely. Find better coverage when what matters is the claim rather than this article. Trace claims, quotes and images back to their original context, since material is often clipped or recaptioned as it spreads.

For scholarly sources the same instinct applies. Check the authors' expertise, read the funding and conflict-of-interest statements, and search the title to see whether the paper has been corrected or retracted.
